message:
A DISCREPANCY IN PW-0312's REVIEW RECORD, recorded rather than left for a reader to find.

gpt-architect's round-94 verdict states the commit it judged: "against authoritative origin: 061df207a6648919c7c3372f8b67640c11eb3434". The review record's machine-readable reviewedCommitSha says c398bd88a856a421ee9b83d98268f91c1dcb9b81. The approve command binds a review to HEAD at the moment it is recorded, and HEAD had moved one commit past what gpt-architect read.

WHY IT MOVED, AND IT WAS NOT CARELESSNESS ABOUT THE REVIEW. c398bd8 is "PW-0501 claimed and started from 061df20" -- a control-plane action taken on gpt-architect's own round-93 instruction to proceed with PW-0501 in parallel and not wait. It was committed before this verdict arrived.

WHY THE BINDING IS STILL SOUND, checked rather than asserted. c398bd8 changes thirteen files: control/events.jsonl, the nine generated agent queues, control/tasks.json, and the two generated coordination views. NONE of them is on PW-0312's allowedPaths or reviewDependencies -- verified by matching every changed path against the declared surface, which returned nothing. So the code, tests, workflow, harness and documentation gpt-architect judged at 061df20 are byte-identical at c398bd8, and the approval is bound to a tree whose reviewed surface is the reviewed surface.

THE EVIDENCE TEXT NAMES 061df20 EXPLICITLY, in both the approval and the security-review gate, so the human-readable record says what was actually read even where the field says something else. That is the part a reviewer should be able to rely on.

THE GENERAL LESSON, worth more than this instance: recording a verdict should come before any other commit, even one the reviewer asked for. "Proceed with PW-0501 in parallel" and "record the verdict first" are not in tension -- they only appeared to be because the verdict arrived after the claim. From here, a verdict is transcribed before anything else in the turn.

NOT CORRECTED BY REWRITING THE FIELD. There is no command to re-bind a recorded review, and hand-editing control/tasks.json to make a machine-readable provenance field say something the tool did not write is exactly the forgery the provenance mechanism exists to make visible. The discrepancy stands with this note beside it.

PL-0406 and PL-AI-0014: acceptance replaced with gpt-architect's round-94 rulings. Both tasks were filed unowned as proposals in round 93 and both are approved; the acceptance each carries is now the reviewer's rather than mine, because a proposal's whole point is that the ruling replaces the proposer's guess.

PL-0406 -- APPROVED as a real P1 defect. gpt-architect confirmed the finding structurally rather than taking my word for the measurement: the documented command runs drizzle-kit migrate, the initial migration was hand-written, the expected journal does not exist, "therefore the documented command can report success while applying no schema."

THE SEVEN-POINT ACCEPTANCE IS THEIRS AND REPLACES MINE, and three of the seven are stronger than what I wrote. I asked for idempotence and loud failure; the ruling adds a regression "proving the old 'exit 0, zero relations' behavior is impossible", a non-zero exit when migration metadata or schema state is invalid, and -- the one I would not have thought to require -- that CI may return to the repaired command ONLY AFTER that evidence exists. My draft left the CI workaround's retirement to whoever fixed the command.

THREE STANDING CONSTRAINTS UNTIL IT IS FIXED, also theirs: do not rely on db:migrate; the direct psql invocation in CI is the approved temporary route; and "keep the eight-table postcondition even after the command itself is repaired." I had argued for that last one and it is now a requirement rather than a preference.

AND A CONSTRAINT ON HOW IT IS FIXED: "Do not silently generate a migration from today's schema if doing so would obscure the reviewed hand-written migration's provenance. Repair the migration mechanism intentionally." That is the same concern my draft raised about PL-0405's review, stated as a rule.

PL-AI-0014 -- filing approved. The acceptance is tightened in one place that matters: my draft required the events file to be unchanged after a refusal, and the ruling requires it "byte-identical", which is the same claim with no room to argue about trailing whitespace. It also adds a clause I had left implicit -- "valid explicit event types still append normally" -- which is the non-vacuity check for the refusal, because a fix that refused everything would satisfy every other clause.

Both acceptances now quote the ruling directly. Neither task is claimed; both remain unowned in BACKLOG, dispatchable when a wave has room.

PW-0501 IMPLEMENTATION COMPLETE, GATES NOT. This is a statement about what cannot be recorded yet and why, written so the task's state is legible rather than looking stalled.

PW-0501's quality gates are `build` and `architecture-review`. NEITHER CAN BE RECORDED FROM THIS SESSION, for different reasons, and neither absence is an oversight.

THE BUILD GATE NEEDS A WINDOWS RUN THAT HAS NOT HAPPENED. This container's Rust toolchain targets x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and the linked machine exposes a Linux VM, so `tauri build` has never executed against this code. The only Windows build machine this project has is the `windows-latest` runner that `.github/workflows/windows.yml` now defines, and that runner sees nothing until the branch reaches origin -- which the git proxy refuses (403, repository not in the session's authorized set; LAST_MILE items 1 and 8). Recording `build` pass from here would be fabricating a gate result, which invariant 8 forbids by name and which round 83 already cost this project once.

THE ARCHITECTURE REVIEW IS gpt-architect's, and a judgement gate is refused to the implementation side before anything is written.

WHAT WAS VERIFIED HERE, AND IT IS MORE THAN THE TOOLCHAIN SUGGESTS:
 - 51 Rust unit tests pass, up from 42. The nine new ones cover the identity guards and the writable layout.
 - `cargo check` AND `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` both pass FOR THE x86_64-pc-windows-msvc TARGET, not only for the host. That target is installed here, so `windows_host.rs` -- which is `cfg(windows)`-gated and invisible to an ordinary Linux build -- is genuinely compiled rather than assumed. The new `data_dir` and `create_directories` implementations are inside that gate and are covered by it.
 - `scripts/windows/artifact-inventory.mjs` was exercised against a fabricated bundle tree in all three branches: the happy path producing two digests, a missing kind, and two installers in one directory (a stale artifact beside a new one).
 - The packaging-script corrective was rehearsed against a real layout: a full `package-sidecar.mjs` run with a stand-in runtime, after which `git status` on `apps/desktop/sidecar` is clean. Before the fix that run deleted two tracked files.
 - `.github/workflows/windows.yml` parses, and the parsed job is confirmed to carry no `continue-on-error` at step or job level and no `|| true` outside comments. The acceptance asks for that by name.

WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED AND MUST NOT BE CLAIMED:
 - that `tauri build` succeeds. The config is valid to `tauri-build` (the crate's build script reads it on every `cargo check`, including the Windows-target one), but a valid config is not a produced installer. WiX and NSIS have never run against this project.
 - the three PowerShell steps. There is no PowerShell in this container -- a `.ps1` cannot even be syntax-checked here -- so the sidecar layout step, the inventory step and the install/uninstall step are unexecuted code.
 - that the MSI installs, that it puts the executable where the workflow asserts it does, or that `Program Files\Project Liberty` is the path WiX chooses from `productName`. That last one is the assertion most likely to be wrong on the first run, and it is written to fail loudly with a directory listing rather than quietly.

ONE TRADE STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. The Tauri CLI is pinned exactly, to 2.12.0, matching the crate's `tauri = "=2.12.0"` -- but the pin lives in the workflow's `env` block and is fetched with `npx`, not held in a lockfile with an integrity hash. `apps/desktop` is not an npm workspace member; the root declares `apps/*`, so giving it a package.json would make it one, pull a large prebuilt binary into `npm ci` for every ubuntu job that does not need it, and change the root lockfile, which is not on this task's surface. Moving it into a lockfile is the better home and is raised rather than quietly preferred.

AND ONE SCOPE ABSENCE THAT IS DELIBERATE. gpt-architect's scope says "clean-install/update/uninstall automation where CI can prove it". Install and uninstall are proven. UPGRADE IS NOT, because an upgrade needs a previous version to upgrade from and this repository has never shipped one -- the first release is what creates the thing a second run could upgrade. PW-0503 owns that matrix.

PW-0501 reviewDependencies: ONE ENTRY GAINED, apps/web/src/app/api/v1/playback/build-target.ts. Read-only; no allowedPath changes. Recorded BEFORE the corrective is written.

WHY. The first Windows run failed, and the fix makes apps/desktop/scripts/package-sidecar.mjs DEPEND ON THE CONTENT of build-target.ts -- it will read `DESKTOP_DIST_DIR` out of that file rather than restating the directory. A reviewer needs that file inside the fingerprinted window to judge whether the derivation is sound, which is exactly what reviewDependencies is for. It stays read-only: nothing in this task writes to apps/web/**.

THE FAILURE, with the run named. Windows package run 36635212507, job 109634058068, head 72e844d, failed at 1m47s in "Lay out the packaged sidecar":

  package-sidecar: no standalone build at D:\a\project-liberty\project-liberty\apps\web\.next\standalone

THE ROOT CAUSE IS A RESTATED PATH, and it is the same defect class the script already guards against in the other direction. `package-sidecar.mjs` reads its input from `apps/web/.next/standalone`. The DESKTOP build does not write there: `next.config.ts` applies `distDirFor(target)`, and `build-target.ts` sets `DESKTOP_DIST_DIR = "dist/desktop"`, so the tree lands at `apps/web/dist/desktop/standalone`. Two files name one location and they disagree.

The script's own header says why that is the defect: "the layout is a contract between three files -- this one, the Rust constants and the Tauri config -- and a contract maintained by hand across three languages is one that drifts." It then VERIFIES its OUTPUT layout against `sidecar.rs` by reading the Rust source and matching the constants. It never verified its INPUT layout against `build-target.ts`. The guard existed on one side of the script and not the other, and the unguarded side is the one that broke.

A SECOND DEFECT BEHIND THE FIRST, found by running the real build rather than by reading. The standalone tree has the monorepo shape: `standalone/apps/web/server.js` with `standalone/node_modules` one level up, and the server's own config says `distDir: "./dist/desktop"` relative to its own directory. The script copies the standalone root into `sidecar/server/`, which would put the entry at `sidecar/server/apps/web/server.js` -- not the `sidecar/server/server.js` that `SERVER_RELATIVE_PATH` names -- and it copies static into `server/.next/static` where the server will look in `server/dist/desktop/static`. The script's closing existence check would have caught the first of those; nothing would have caught the second, because a server that starts and serves pages with no CSS is not a crash.

AND A FINDING ABOUT MY OWN VERIFICATION, which is the reason this reached CI at all. In round 94 I rehearsed the packaging script locally and reported it as passing. It passed because an EMPTY `apps/web/.next/standalone` directory was sitting in my working tree -- left by a stub I had created minutes earlier while testing the tracked-file corrective, then partly cleaned up. `existsSync` on an empty directory is true, so the input check passed against a directory containing nothing. The rehearsal measured my own leftovers. A clean checkout has no such directory, which is what CI is for and what it did.

CONFLICT CHECK. build-target.ts is covered by PL-0501, DONE, and is read-only here. No active task claims it. PW-0501 remains the only task not in a terminal state apart from the three BLOCKED ones.

A SECOND DEFECT, FOUND BY RUNNING THE PACKAGED SIDECAR RATHER THAN BY READING IT, and it is worse than the one that failed CI: the installed application would answer 403 to every request the WebView makes, and the window would be blank.

HOW IT WAS FOUND. After correcting the packaging script I started the packaged tree directly -- the real `sidecar/node.exe server/server.js`, laid out by the real script from a real desktop build -- and drove it with curl using the launch environment `plan_launch` produces. Everything returned 403 with no body, which is `proxy.ts`'s refusal shape exactly.

THE MISMATCH, IN THREE LINES:
 - `sidecar.rs` sets HOST_VAR (LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST) to BIND_HOST, the literal "127.0.0.1", with no port. It also sets PORT to BIND_PORT, the literal "0", so the listener takes an EPHEMERAL port.
 - `policy.ts`'s `authorizeRequest` compares that value against the request's `Host` header with `!==`, and its own comment insists the comparison must be exact: "127.0.0.1:3000 and 127.0.0.1:3001 are different listeners and a comparison that ignored the port would accept a request meant for another."
 - A `Host` header from any client always carries a non-default port. So the comparison is "127.0.0.1:<ephemeral>" against "127.0.0.1", which can never match.

`policy.test.ts` uses `const HOST = "127.0.0.1:3100"` -- host AND port. The policy side was written expecting an authority; the shell side sends a bare hostname. Each half is self-consistent and the pair is not, which is why both suites pass.

PROVEN BY A CONTROLLED COMPARISON, one variable changed:
 - LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST="127.0.0.1"      -> /api/health 403, / 403, stylesheet 403, client chunk 403.
 - LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST="127.0.0.1:3211" -> /api/health 200, / 200 (14612 bytes), stylesheet 200 (8085 bytes), client chunk 200 (9871 bytes).
Same packaged tree, same token, same binary, same port. Only the expected-host value differs.

THE SECOND RESULT IS ALSO THE FIRST END-TO-END EVIDENCE THIS PROJECT HAS that the packaged sidecar works at all: a standalone Next server, laid out by the packaging script from a desktop build, serving its own pages, its stylesheet and its client chunks from the flattened `server/` layout with `node_modules` beside it. That is the layout question the packaging corrective was about, answered by observation.

WHY NO TEST CAUGHT IT. Both sides are unit-tested and neither test can see the other: `policy.test.ts` supplies its own expected host, and `sidecar.rs`'s tests assert that HOST_VAR equals BIND_HOST -- which is the defect written down as an expectation, the same shape as the fall-through test PW-0312 deleted last round. Nothing in the repository composes the shell's env with the sidecar's gate, because until this round nothing could: there was no packaged sidecar to start.

THE ORDERING PROBLEM BEHIND IT, which is why the fix is not a one-word change. The expected host must contain the port, and with PORT=0 the port does not exist until after the child has bound it. The shell learns it from the handshake on stdout -- too late, because the child's environment is fixed at spawn.

WHAT I AM NOT DOING. Not relaxing `authorizeRequest` to compare only the hostname. `policy.ts` is not on this task's surface, and more importantly its comment rejects that explicitly: dropping the port would accept a request meant for a different listener. The control is right; the value handed to it is wrong.

SCOPE. `sidecar.rs` and `shell.rs` are both under `apps/desktop/**`, already on PW-0501's allowedPaths, so the corrective needs no surface amendment. `policy.ts` is untouched.

PW-0105 CREATED UNOWNED AS A PROPOSAL FOR gpt-architect, round 95. P0, lane Player. "The sidecar half of the desktop contract was never wired into the server."

WHAT IT IS. PW-0101 designed the sidecar contract and PW-0102 built the shell that speaks it. Nothing connected the other half. Three symptoms, one cause, all found by STARTING THE PACKAGED ARTEFACT -- which this project had never done until the packaging corrective in this round made a startable one:

 1. The handshake line is never emitted. formatHandshake's only caller is its own test; the packaged server's whole stdout is Next's banner and the catalog line. shell.rs waits, times out, kills the child, reports NoHandshake. The installed application never opens a window on content.
 2. The expected host can never match. sidecar.rs sends a bare "127.0.0.1"; policy.ts compares it to a Host header that always carries a port, and its own test uses "127.0.0.1:3100". Proven with a one-variable comparison against the packaged tree: bare -> 403 everywhere; with the port -> 200 on five routes plus the stylesheet and a client chunk.
 3. checkBindSafety -- the control that refuses to start a sidecar bound to 0.0.0.0 -- is written, tested, and called by nothing.

WHY THIS IS A RULING AND NOT A PATCH. Symptom 2 has an ordering problem behind it: the expected host needs the port, BIND_PORT is "0", and the port does not exist until the child binds. handshake.ts records why that was chosen, in terms -- the shell picking a port has a TOCTOU window and "the user sees a blank window". So the fix is one of three architecture decisions: the sidecar derives its own authority after binding, the shell reserves a port and a reviewed decision is reversed, or the comparison changes shape against its own comment's argument. I have not picked one.

WHY EVERY EXISTING TEST PASSES. Each half is unit-tested against its own fixture and neither can see the other. That is the same shape as the defect PW-0312 deleted last round -- a test asserting the defect as an expectation -- and the acceptance therefore REQUIRES a test that composes the two halves rather than a third self-consistent one.

THE SURFACE SPANS BOTH SIDES, deliberately. A task confined to apps/web or to apps/desktop would reproduce the two-self-consistent-halves problem that caused this. It overlaps PW-0501's apps/desktop/**, so the two must not be active together; resolved by sequence, as PW-0102 and PW-0501 were.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT TAKE AWAY FROM PW-0501. That task proves CI produces an installer, that it installs and uninstalls, and -- as of this round -- that the packaged tree serves its pages, stylesheet and client chunks when given a correct environment. It has never claimed the application launches, and windows.yml says so in its header. The two findings are complementary: PW-0501 makes a package, PW-0105 makes it start.

FOUR PROPOSALS NOW STAND UNOWNED: PL-0406 and PL-AI-0014 (both approved in round 94, acceptance carrying gpt-architect's rulings) and PW-0105 (this one, awaiting a ruling).

PW-0105 RULING RECORDED, transcribed by claude-lead from gpt-architect's round-95 verdict. "PW-0105 RULING - proceed."

THE DESIGN QUESTION I RAISED IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS THE OPTION I DID NOT PROPOSE. I offered three: the sidecar derives its own authority after binding; the shell reserves a port; the comparison changes shape. gpt-architect rejected the second in terms -- "Do NOT replace the kernel-selected-port design with shell-selected/free-port probing" -- and then did something better than choosing between the other two: "Instead, amend the contract."

THE CONTRADICTION, IN THEIR WORDS: "PW-0101 says the kernel chooses the port and the child reports it after bind. authorizeRequest expects LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST to equal the full incoming Host literal, including the port. The shell cannot know that full authority before the kernel chooses the port." The resolution is that LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST "should represent the expected HOSTNAME / loopback identity, not a precomputed <host>:<unknown-port> authority."

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE SHELL, and it is the part worth stating early: the value sidecar.rs already sends -- BIND_HOST, the bare literal "127.0.0.1" -- BECOMES CORRECT UNDER THE AMENDED CONTRACT. What I recorded as the shell sending the wrong thing is, after the amendment, the shell sending the right thing to a gate that was reading it wrongly. The defect is entirely on the sidecar side.

EIGHT INVARIANTS TO PRESERVE, quoted so a later round cannot erode one by accident:
 1. The sidecar binds only to an explicit loopback address, preferably 127.0.0.1.
 2. PORT=0 remains the normal launch contract. The OS/kernel chooses the port.
 3. The shell generates a fresh per-launch CSPRNG token and passes it through the environment, never argv.
 4. The shell does not show the application window until it receives and validates the sidecar handshake.
 5. A non-loopback bind is a hard startup refusal.
 6. A missing/invalid token is a hard startup refusal.
 7. DNS-rebinding protection remains mandatory.
 8. No sidecar security control may exist only as an unused helper.

The eighth is the one this whole task exists for, and it generalises the finding rather than restating it: checkBindSafety was written, tested and unreachable, and that is now a rule rather than an incident.

FOUR REQUIREMENTS:
 A. checkBindSafety(readSidecarEnvironment(process.env)) must run on the real startup path BEFORE the listener becomes externally usable. On failure: do not continue serving, emit an actionable local diagnostic, exit non-zero, "never silently downgrade."
 B. The actual listener emits exactly one machine-readable line once bound, carrying the ACTUAL port: "Do not infer the reported port from the requested PORT=0; obtain the actual bound port from the listening server." Not before successful bind.
 C. Host validation becomes hostname-exact: parse the Host header safely, require the hostname to match the configured loopback host exactly, and reject "DNS names, suffix matches, alternate hosts, 0.0.0.0, LAN addresses, malformed authorities, and userinfo-style tricks". IF the runtime can reliably obtain the actual local listening port, ALSO require the Host port to equal it -- "from runtime listener/request facts, not from a pre-spawn environment guess". If it cannot, hostname-exact plus the per-launch token is the required minimum AND the reason must be documented. "Do NOT weaken this to suffix matching or includes(\"127.0.0.1\")."
 D. Sixteen named regression properties, covering the whole contract rather than the helpers.

AND AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT HOW TO VERIFY, which lands directly on my round-94 mistake: "After implementing PW-0105, run the real packaged sidecar again, not a stubbed rehearsal. Clean or isolate the output directory first so stale build artifacts cannot satisfy existence checks." That is the empty-.next/standalone trap written as a standing procedure.

ON PW-0501: "First deliver the already-prepared PW-0501 packaging corrective: 72e844d -> 65a47d5." Delivered; Diego applies and pushes. "Do not call PW-0501 DONE merely because an installer is produced. A green package run proves the packaging/build gate, not installed runtime correctness."

PW-0105 allowedPaths: NARROWED, before any file is written. Two entries removed: apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/sidecar.rs and apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/shell.rs. One added: apps/web/src/lib/server-bootstrap.ts.

WHY THE RUST SIDE COMES OUT. I put it in when I proposed the task, because the shell appeared to be sending the wrong value. gpt-architect's ruling amends the CONTRACT instead: LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST "should represent the expected HOSTNAME / loopback identity, not a precomputed <host>:<unknown-port> authority". Under that amendment `sidecar.rs`'s BIND_HOST -- the bare literal "127.0.0.1" -- is already exactly right, and the test asserting HOST_VAR equals BIND_HOST stops being a defect written down as an expectation and becomes a correct assertion about the amended contract. There is nothing for this task to change there.

Keeping the paths reserved anyway would be a reservation nothing needs, which is the precedent PW-0312 applied four times. It also has a second cost here that a reservation usually does not: those paths overlap PW-0501's apps/desktop/**, and PW-0501 is IN_PROGRESS. Holding them would force the two tasks into a sequence gpt-architect's ruling does not ask for -- the verdict says "Keep PW-0501 and PW-0105 separate", which is about not conflating their evidence, not about serialising them. Narrowed, they are disjoint and both can proceed.

WHY server-bootstrap.ts COMES IN. Requirement A puts checkBindSafety on the real startup path, and requirement B puts the handshake there too. `instrumentation.ts` is a framework convention file whose own header states the rule this task must not break: "THERE IS NO LOGIC HERE, AND THAT IS THE POINT. Everything this file could get wrong ... lives in lib/server-bootstrap.ts, where server-bootstrap.test.ts drives it. A framework convention file is the one place in an application that no test can call, so it should hold nothing worth testing." Putting a security gate and a port handshake into the convention file would put the two most testable things in this task in the one file no test can reach. They go in server-bootstrap.ts; instrumentation.ts gains a call and nothing else.

IF THE RUST SIDE TURNS OUT TO NEED A CHANGE AFTER ALL -- a comment that now describes the superseded contract, say -- it will be raised rather than taken, because those paths will not be on this surface.

CONFLICT CHECKED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. apps/web/src/lib/server-bootstrap.ts is covered by PL-0308, DONE, and by PL-0305, DONE. apps/web/src/lib/sidecar/** and apps/web/src/instrumentation.ts are covered by PW-0101 and PL-0308, both DONE. No active task claims any of them, and after this narrowing PW-0105 and PW-0501 share no path.

PW-0105 allowedPaths: WIDENED BY TWO ENTRIES, before any file is written.

MOVED FROM reviewDependencies TO allowedPaths:
  apps/web/src/proxy.ts
  docs/DESKTOP_PLAYBACK.md

WHY proxy.ts. Requirement C makes the actual listening port part of the Host
decision, "from runtime listener/request facts, not from a pre-spawn environment
guess". authorizeRequest is documented as PURE -- it reads no process, no clock --
and a pure function cannot discover a listener. The alternatives were (a) a
defaulted third parameter that silently evaluates to null wherever the caller was
not updated, which is the silent downgrade the ruling forbids by name, or (b) hidden
mutable module state in policy.ts, which is worse than an argument and is not
reliable across Next's separate node-runtime bundles. So the port arrives as a
REQUIRED third argument and proxy.ts -- the one call site -- supplies it. That is a
two-line change to a file the ruling already put in the review fingerprint.

WHY DESKTOP_PLAYBACK.md. The ruling amends a published contract: LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST
"should represent the expected HOSTNAME / loopback identity, not a precomputed
<host>:<unknown-port> authority". Sections 2 and 7 currently state the old reading.
Leaving the document stating a contract the code no longer implements is how the next
round re-derives the defect from the documentation.

CONFLICT CHECK, BOTH DIRECTIONS. The only other active task is PW-0501 (claude-infra,
IN_PROGRESS) with allowedPaths [".github/workflows/windows.yml","apps/desktop/**",
"scripts/windows/**"]. Neither new entry is under any of those, and neither new entry
is claimed by any other CLAIMED/IN_PROGRESS/REVIEW task. PW-0501 keeps
apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/handshake.rs and sidecar.rs; PW-0105 does not write Rust.
No Rust change is required: the shell already sends LIBERTY_SIDECAR_HOST=BIND_HOST
("127.0.0.1"), which the amended contract makes correct, and the handshake line's

THE ORIGINAL INVARIANT IS RESTATED RATHER THAN RELAXED, in five clauses: the shell must NOT probe for or
preselect a free TCP port; the sidecar binds loopback only; the OPERATING SYSTEM chooses the port; the
sidecar reports the ACTUAL bound port to the shell; the shell uses that reported port for the webview
origin. My candidate (c) -- a shell-chosen port with a retry loop -- is rejected, as expected, and my
candidate (b) -- post-processing the generated entry -- is allowed only as a last resort.

THE REQUIRED DIRECTION, and it is candidate (a): "make the packaged desktop sidecar own the listener
bootstrap at the point where an actual Node `Server` is available."
 1. Keep the Next application/standalone output as the request handler.
 2. Introduce the SMALLEST SUPPORTED desktop-specific bootstrap that creates the HTTP listener explicitly
    on host 127.0.0.1, port 0.
 3. Read the actual port from `server.address()` after the listen callback/event.
 4. Emit the existing single handshake line with that port.
 5. Preserve every PW-0105 control: per-launch token, request authorization, Host validation, bind-safety,
    fail-closed, no LAN bind, no source-checkout dependency.
 6. "Do not patch generated Next output after every build unless there is no stable supported composition
    point. Prefer a checked-in desktop bootstrap that consumes the generated standalone application."
 7. THE STOP CONDITION, quoted because it governs what I do if the public API does not reach: "If Next's
    public/server APIs make that impossible without depending on unstable internals, stop and document the
    exact API limitation before choosing another design. Do not silently couple us to generated
    implementation details."

TWELVE PIECES OF ACCEPTANCE EVIDENCE: launch with 3000 deliberately occupied; the packaged sidecar still
starts; the actual listener port is not 3000 in that test; the handshake contains the real bound port; the
shell parser accepts it; all required routes serve; static/CSS/client assets load; token and Host attack
cases still fail; non-loopback startup fails; nothing writes beside the executable; repeated launches can
use DIFFERENT kernel-selected ports; no shell-side free-port probing exists. Plus regression coverage
"specifically preventing PORT=0 from silently becoming 3000 again".

ON TASK SEPARATION, which is the part that constrains the board rather than the code: "Keep PW-0501,
PW-0105, and PW-0106 separate" -- packaging/installability, sidecar security/handshake contract, and
kernel-selected listener port respectively. "PW-0106 must not be folded into either task merely to make

PW-0106 API INVESTIGATION COMPLETE, and it answers gpt-architect's requirement 7 in advance: "If Next's
public/server APIs make that impossible without depending on unstable internals, stop and document the
exact API limitation before choosing another design."

THE ANSWER IS: THE DESIGN WORKS, AND IT NEEDS EXACTLY ONE NON-PUBLIC COUPLING. Measured against the real
packaged sidecar, not read from documentation.

WHAT IS PUBLIC AND SUFFICIENT.
  const next = require("next");
  const app  = next({ dir, dev: false, hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: 0 });
  const handler = app.getRequestHandler();
  const server  = http.createServer(...handler...);
  server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => { server.address().port });
`next()` is the documented custom-server entry point and `getRequestHandler()` is documented API. WE own
the listener, so the kernel chooses the port and `server.address()` reports it. That is requirement 2
and 3 met with nothing internal.

THE ORDERING THAT MAKES IT WORK, and it is not incidental: LISTEN FIRST, PREPARE SECOND. The http handler
awaits the `prepare()` promise, `listen(0)` runs in the same tick, and `app.prepare()` is called from the
listen callback. Two consequences, both good. PW-0105's instrumentation runs during `prepare()`, which is
now AFTER the bind, so its handle-table discovery finds the listener exactly as it does today -- NO
PW-0105 CODE CHANGES ARE REQUIRED. And no request can be served before `prepare()` resolves, so the
bind-safety check genuinely precedes the first served request. That STRENGTHENS PW-0105 requirement A,
whose residual window I reported last round.

THE ONE THING THE PUBLIC API DOES NOT REACH: THE RESOLVED CONFIG.
`next({ conf })` accepts a `conf` option in its TYPES -- `NextServerOptions` is
`Omit<ServerOptions, "conf"> & Partial<Pick<ServerOptions, "conf">>`. It is SILENTLY IGNORED on this path.
`createServer()` returns `NextCustomServer` whenever `customServer !== false`, and
`NextCustomServer.prepare()` calls `getRequestHandlers({ dir, port, isDev, hostname, minimalMode, quiet })`
-- `conf` is not among the forwarded fields. Verified empirically: passing the correct config produced
"Could not find a production build in the '.next' directory", i.e. `distDir` fell back to the default
while our build writes `dist/desktop`. A typed option that does nothing is worse than an absent one, and
this is the exact API limitation requirement 7 asked me to name.

TWO WAYS ROUND IT WERE BUILT AND RUN.

  VARIANT A -- a `next.config.js` in the packaged server directory, exporting the config from
  `<distDir>/required-server-files.json`. FULLY PUBLIC, AND IT SERVES. Rejected anyway, for two measured
  reasons. (1) `loadConfig` re-runs `assignDefaults` over an already-resolved config and DROPS keys:
  observed warnings name `htmlLimitedBots` ("Input not instance of RegExp" -- a serialized RegExp cannot
  round-trip through JSON), `experimental.trustHostHeader`, `experimental.turbopackMemoryEvictionMode`,
  `experimental.isExperimentalCompile`, plus `configFileName`, `repoRoot` and `distDirRoot`. Silently
  serving with a runtime config that differs from the built one is the class of defect this project
  spends its rounds finding. (2) `loadConfig` calls `loadWebpackHook()`, whose failure is caught ONLY when
  the standalone path is active -- Next's own comment: "this can fail in standalone mode as the files
  aren't traced/included". A more aggressively traced tree would throw here.

  VARIANT B -- set `process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG` from the same manifest before requiring
  `next`. This is the mechanism NEXT'S OWN generated standalone entry uses, and `config.js` short-circuits
  on it with the comment "we don't apply assignDefaults or modifyConfig here as it has already been
  applied". No re-normalisation, no dropped keys, no warnings, and the `loadWebpackHook` guard is armed.
  It is a private double-underscore env var: THE ONE NON-PUBLIC COUPLING, and the implementation must
  assert at startup that it took effect so a future Next that removes it fails loudly rather than serving
  on defaults.

Note what variant B is NOT: it does not read, parse, patch or depend on the generated `server.js`. The
config comes from `<distDir>/required-server-files.json`, a build-output MANIFEST, which is also where
Next's own `next start` looks for the serialized build config. Requirement 6 is satisfied -- a checked-in
bootstrap consuming the generated standalone application, with no post-build patching.

message:
PW-0106 DEPENDENCY-RISK ANALYSIS for `__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG`, performed before the design is
treated as settled, because "the prototype works" is not an approval. Seven questions, answered against
the installed package rather than from memory.

1. EXACT NEXT VERSION. next@16.3.1, resolved at /home/claude/liberty/node_modules/next. The packaged
   sidecar carries its own copy of the same version at
   apps/desktop/sidecar/server/node_modules/next.

2. EXACT SOURCE LOCATIONS CONSUMING IT, from a grep over the shipped dist (.js only; the .map files
   and the esm mirror are the same code):
     next/dist/server/config.js   -- 3 occurrences. Two matter:
        (a) line ~1379, inside `loadConfigImpl`: the failure of `loadWebpackHook()` is swallowed ONLY
            when this variable is set, with the comment "this can fail in standalone mode as the files
            aren't traced/included";
        (b) line ~1384: the short-circuit that returns the pre-resolved config, with the comment
            "we don't apply assignDefaults or modifyConfig here as it has already been applied".
     next/dist/server/next.js     -- 1 occurrence: suppresses the "next start does not work with
            output: standalone" warning.
     next/dist/build/utils.js     -- 1 occurrence, line 1130, and it is the important one: it is the
            TEMPLATE that Next's own build writes into the generated standalone `server.js`.

3. UPSTREAM TEST COVERAGE: UNKNOWN AND I WILL NOT GUESS. The published npm package ships no tests, and
   this session cannot reach the Next repository to look. What can be established from the artifact is
   weaker but real: the variable is referenced from three independent modules, one of which is the
   build-time generator, and the standalone output does not function without it. That is evidence of
   load-bearing status, NOT evidence of a test guarding it. Stated as a gap rather than rounded up.

4. IS IT INTENTIONALLY USED BY GENERATED STANDALONE OUTPUT? YES, and this is the decisive finding.
   `dist/build/utils.js` emits, verbatim, into every standalone entry Next generates:
       const nextConfig = ${JSON.stringify(nextConfig)}
       process.env.__NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG = JSON.stringify(nextConfig)
       require('next')
   So the variable is not a back door found by reading internals; it is the channel Next's own
   supported standalone deployment uses, written by Next's own build. Our bootstrap sets the same
   variable to the same value from the same build's manifest.

5. IS THERE A SUPPORTED ALTERNATIVE THAT DOES NOT CORRUPT OR RE-RESOLVE THE CONFIG? NO. Three were
   examined and each fails on a measured fact:
     - `next({ conf })`: typed (`NextServerOptions` makes `conf` optional) and SILENTLY IGNORED.
       `createServer()` returns `NextCustomServer` whenever `customServer !== false`, and
       `NextCustomServer.prepare()` calls
       `getRequestHandlers({ dir, port, isDev, onDevServerCleanup, hostname, minimalMode, quiet })`.
       `conf` is not in that object. Verified empirically: the server looked for a build in `.next`.
     - `startServer({ config })` from `next/dist/server/lib/start-server`: ALSO IGNORED, and this is
       the finding that closes the question. Its signature destructures
       `{ dir, isDev, hostname, minimalMode, allowRetry, keepAliveTimeout, selfSignedCertificate,
       serverFastRefresh }` -- no `config` -- and `getRequestHandlers` does not accept one either.
       Next's generated entry passes `config: nextConfig` to `startServer` AND that argument goes
       nowhere; the env var on the line above is what actually delivers the config. So even Next's own
       supported standalone path depends on this variable exclusively.
     - a `next.config.js` in the packaged directory: public, and it serves, but `loadConfig` re-runs
       `assignDefaults` over an already-resolved config and DROPS keys. Observed warnings named
       `htmlLimitedBots` ("Input not instance of RegExp" -- a serialized RegExp cannot round-trip
       through JSON), `experimental.trustHostHeader`, `experimental.turbopackMemoryEvictionMode`,
       `experimental.isExperimentalCompile`, `configFileName`, `repoRoot`, `distDirRoot`. It also
       re-arms `loadWebpackHook`, whose failure is caught only on the standalone path. Serving with a
       runtime config that silently differs from the built one is a worse dependency than a named one.

6. WHAT BREAKS IF NEXT CHANGES OR REMOVES IT. `loadConfig` stops short-circuiting, `assignDefaults`
   runs over nothing, `distDir` becomes the default `.next`, and the server looks for a build that is
   not there. On this version that surfaces as `prepare()` rejecting with "Could not find a production
   build in the '.next' directory" -- loud. A future version could instead resolve a partial default
   config and SERVE on it, which would be silent and much worse: wrong image config, wrong
   `htmlLimitedBots`, wrong experimental flags, with no error.

7. HOW OUR REGRESSION TESTS DETECT IT IMMEDIATELY. Three layers, deliberately arranged so the earliest
   one is a build failure rather than a runtime one:
     - PACKAGING TIME, the new one and the one that matters:
       `assertStandaloneConfigChannelStillExists` in `package-sidecar.mjs` reads the SHIPPED copy of
       `server/node_modules/next/dist/server/config.js` and fails the packaging step if it no longer
       names the variable. A Next upgrade that removes the channel therefore turns into a red build
       before any artifact exists, and the failure message names this analysis.
     - STARTUP TIME: `liberty-sidecar.js` verifies the layout file and the build manifest agree on
       `distDir` and that `<distDir>/BUILD_ID` exists, then `explainPrepareFailure` rewrites Next's
       `.next` error into one that names the coupling and says not to "fix" it by moving the build.
     - ACCEPTANCE TIME: `acceptance.mjs` item 2 fails if the packaged sidecar does not start.

CONCLUSION, AND WHAT I AM NOT DOING WITH IT. On the evidence above the private variable is the smallest
viable solution: it is the only channel that exists, it is the one Next's own build writes, and every
public alternative either does nothing or silently mutates the config. It is NOT being treated as
permanent architecture. It is one named coupling, guarded at packaging time against the exact copy that
ships, documented in the file that uses it, and PUT TO gpt-architect FOR AN EXPLICIT RULING in the
round-98 handoff. If they refuse it, the fallback is the `next.config.js` variant plus an enumerated
list of the keys it drops -- worse, but available, and a decision rather than a discovery.

     - `the_shell_states_a_kernel_chosen_port_and_never_a_number_it_picked`: BIND_PORT is "0", the

   missing_and_where` matched the literal "server.js" to simulate an absent server. After the entry
   was renamed that predicate matched nothing, so the test got a valid launch and would have claimed a
   missing-server error it never saw -- a test that renames itself out of its own assertion. It now
   derives the filename from SERVER_RELATIVE_PATH.

2. `npm run test` -> 22/22 turbo tasks; @liberty/web 74 files / 1308 tests, @liberty/backend 3 files /
   36 tests, all passing. Unchanged by this task by design: PW-0106 touched no TypeScript, and

3. `node apps/desktop/sidecar-bootstrap/acceptance.mjs` -> 13/13, against the REAL packaged sidecar.
   This is where the actual acceptance lives and it is a script rather than a unit test for a reason
   stated in its header: the defect is in Next's generated entry, is invisible to every test in this
   repository, and was found by starting the artifact. A test that could not have found it is not the
   test this task needs. Results:
     1  port 3000 occupied for the test                held by the harness itself
     2  the packaged sidecar starts with 3000 occupied a handshake was emitted
     3  the actual listener port is not 3000           bound 40197
     4  the handshake carries the REAL bound port      GET /api/health on 40197 -> 200
     5  the handshake satisfies the parser grammar     {"host":"127.0.0.1","port":40197}
     6  all required routes serve                      / /search /profiles /api/health /signin all 200
     7  static / CSS / client assets load              stylesheet 200 (8085 B), chunk 200 (9871 B)
     8  token and Host attack cases still fail         8 cases, all 403: no token, wrong token,
                                                       evil.test, 127.0.0.1.evil.test, userinfo,

                                                       and HOSTNAME unset: exit 1, no handshake, each

4. PACKAGING-TIME ASSERTIONS, which run on every `package-sidecar.mjs` invocation including the Windows

THE DEFECT, REPRODUCED HERE FIRST, against PostgreSQL 16.15 on a real connection string. Before the
fix, on a fresh empty database, `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence` left ZERO relations. One
correction to the record, because the exact failure shape decides what the regression has to assert:
on drizzle-kit 0.31.10 with NO journal the command exits **1**, not 0, and prints NOTHING on stderr --
a silent non-zero. The reported "exit 0, zero relations" is reproducible too, and it is the WORSE
neighbouring case: a journal that exists with `entries: []` prints "migrations applied successfully!",
exits 0, and creates nothing. Both are now impossible; I am recording the distinction rather than
repeating a measurement I did not make.

THE REPAIR, AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO. `drizzle-kit migrate` does not read a directory of
`.sql` files; it reads `meta/_journal.json` and applies the tags listed there. That directory held the
hand-written `0000_profile_scoped_identity.sql` and nothing else. The fix adds the missing metadata:
`migrations/meta/_journal.json` naming the existing file, and `migrations/meta/0000_snapshot.json`.
THE REVIEWED SQL IS BYTE-FOR-BYTE UNTOUCHED, which is the constraint gpt-architect set -- "Do not
silently generate a migration from today's schema if doing so would obscure the reviewed hand-written
migration's provenance." The snapshot was obtained by running `drizzle-kit generate` into a THROWAWAY
directory outside the repository and copying only `meta/0000_snapshot.json` across; the SQL that run
produced was discarded. The journal's `when` is 1787588559000 -- the author date of commit 1dd8e73,
which added the migration -- not the time this repair was typed.

THE SEVEN ACCEPTANCE ITEMS:
 1. fresh empty PostgreSQL database                  lib_final, 0 relations before
 2. the documented command                           `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence`
 3. it ACTUALLY CREATES the expected schema           exit 0, 8 tables: account,
                                                      active_profile_selection, playback_progress,
                                                      profile, session, user, verification,
                                                      watchlist_entry
 4. a second invocation is safely idempotent          exit 0, still 8 tables, drizzle ledger still 1 row
 5. NON-ZERO on invalid metadata or schema state      measured, four cases: no journal -> 1;
                                                      malformed journal JSON -> 1; journal tag with no
                                                      matching .sql -> 1; and the one that does NOT
                                                      fail, `entries: []` -> 0 with zero tables, which
                                                      is why item 6 asserts non-emptiness rather than
                                                      mere existence
 6. a regression proving the old behaviour impossible `src/migration-journal.test.ts`, 8 tests, and
                                                      PROVEN NON-VACUOUS by mutation: `entries: []`
                                                      turns 2 red, deleting the journal turns 7 red,
                                                      removing the snapshot turns 1 red, and restoring
                                                      each returns 8 green
 7. CI may return to the repaired command only after  NOT DONE HERE, and deliberately.
    that evidence exists                              `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is a reviewDependency
                                                      of this task, read-only. The evidence now exists;
                                                      the switch is proposed in the handoff.

THE EIGHT-TABLE POSTCONDITION IS KEPT, as required -- asserted in the test against the SQL so it runs
in the unit job without a database, and separately observed against the live one above.

TWO THINGS MEASURED THAT ARE WORTH THE RECORD. `db:check` is NOT a guard for this: with the journal
present and no snapshot it answered "Everything's fine". And a journal WITHOUT a snapshot makes the
next `db:generate` emit a duplicate migration re-creating all eight tables -- observed as
`0001_nervous_omega_red.sql` in a throwaway copy; with the snapshot installed the same command answers
"No schema changes, nothing to migrate". That is why the snapshot is part of the repair and why the
test asserts one per entry.

The five hand-written CHECK constraints survive the migration and are visible in the live database:
playback_progress_epoch_positive, playback_progress_position_non_negative,
playback_progress_position_within_runtime, playback_progress_runtime_positive,
playback_progress_seq_non_negative.

PL-0407 CREATED UNOWNED AS A PROPOSAL FOR gpt-architect. P2, lane Backend, BACKLOG.

"The Drizzle snapshot names three primary keys the database does not have."

Found while repairing PL-0406 and deliberately not folded into it: PL-0406's acceptance puts changing
the schema and adding a second migration out of scope, and every available remedy needs one or the
other. Folding it in would also have meant editing `src/schema/index.ts`, which PL-0405 reviewed.

P2 rather than P1 because nothing is broken today -- the eight tables exist, the constraints are
enforced, and `drizzle-kit generate` never consults a database. It becomes a P1 the day someone
generates a migration that touches a primary key, at which point it fails against every real database
at once. Three remedies are enumerated in the notes with their costs; (a), naming the constraints in
the ORM schema, looks right and is not being taken unilaterally.

The notes also name what should have caught it: `db:check` answers "Everything's fine" because it
validates the journal, not the agreement between a snapshot and a migrated database.

THE TYPECHECK MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED THE DESIGN, and it is the one that makes untracking safe rather than merely idiomatic. The acceptance offers untracking as a candidate and warns it "changes what a fresh clone must do". Measured on this tree, twice:

  - `apps/web/next-env.d.ts` absent, `apps/web/.next/` absent -- the exact fresh-clone condition --
    `npx tsc --noEmit -p apps/web/tsconfig.json` exits 0.
  - `next-env.d.ts` present but carrying the DESKTOP spelling, with `apps/web/dist/desktop/dev/`
    not existing, `tsc --noEmit` exits 0.

So a fresh clone typechecks with the file missing, and a developer whose last invocation was a desktop one typechecks with it stale. `tsconfig.json` lists the file under `include`, and an `include` entry that matches nothing is not an error -- only `files` is. Neither case needs a cleanup step, which is what lets the restore be deleted rather than hardened.

message:
PW-0106 PRIVATE-API RULING RECORDED, transcribed by claude-lead from gpt-architect's round-98 verdict.
"The narrowly isolated use of __NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE_CONFIG is APPROVED for the current pinned Next
implementation, subject to the containment already implemented."

WHAT THE APPROVAL IS, IN THEIR WORDS, AND IT IS NARROWER THAN "APPROVED": "This is a VERSION-BOUND
COMPATIBILITY ADAPTER, not general permission to depend on arbitrary private Next APIs." The clause
matters more than the verdict, and it is the reason this is recorded as its own event rather than
folded into the gate: a later round looking for precedent must find the boundary, not just the yes.

THE CONTAINMENT THEY REVIEWED, enumerated by them: the desktop bootstrap owns the HTTP listener; it
binds literal port 0 on explicit loopback; the actual port comes from `server.address()` after a
successful bind; Next is constructed with that real port, not 0; the bootstrap does not read
`process.env.PORT`; resolved configuration comes from the packaged `required-server-files.json`; the
generated `server.js` is neither patched nor spawned; packaging examines the ACTUAL SHIPPED Next
bytes and fails if `dist/server/config.js` stops consuming the variable; missing or malformed build
configuration fails closed with an actionable diagnostic; the acceptance harness deliberately occupies
port 3000 and verifies real runtime behaviour; and the dependency is documented rather than hidden.

SIX STANDING CONDITIONS, which outlive this task and bind future rounds:
 1. Preserve the packaging guard against the shipped Next bytes.
 2. Preserve the runtime fail-closed diagnostics.
 3. A NEXT VERSION UPGRADE THAT TOUCHES THIS CONTRACT REQUIRES PW-0106 REQUALIFICATION BEFORE RELEASE.
 4. If Next provides a stable public mechanism that preserves the resolved standalone configuration
    correctly, MIGRATE TO IT.
 5. Do not patch or parse generated `server.js` to preserve this behaviour.
 6. Do not replace kernel-selected port allocation with shell-side probing.

Condition 3 is the one with a release-process consequence rather than a code one, and nothing in this
repository enforces it today: `next` is pinned in package.json, and a version bump is an ordinary
dependency change that no gate ties back to PW-0106. The packaging guard catches the case where the
variable DISAPPEARS; it does not catch a version that still reads the variable but changes what the
resolved config must contain. That gap is stated here rather than assumed closed, and a follow-up
that makes the Next version a declared input of PW-0106's requalification is worth proposing once the
task is DONE.

list from `.gitignore` (the file is a pattern language, and a partial reimplementation of it inside a
test harness is a new defect surface), and copying with `git archive` instead of `fs.cpSync` (correct

PL-AI-0015 now waits on PL-AI-0014's, and three documentation corrections are queued behind PW-0105,
PW-0106 and PL-0406. The mechanism is correct -- a review must bind to what was reviewed -- but its

PL-0407 RECOMMENDATION PREPARED, NOT IMPLEMENTED. gpt-architect asked for an architecture/risk
recommendation and said not to repair silently where a ruling is required. A ruling IS required here:
the remedy I would pick edits `packages/persistence/src/schema/`, the module PL-0405 reviewed, and
PL-0406's acceptance put "changing the schema" out of scope for exactly that reason.

(A note on the previous architecture.recommendation event, which is append-only and therefore stands:
the word rendered as "читable" in it is a typo for "readable". Recorded here rather than left as a
puzzle for whoever reads the log next.)

THE DEFECT, RESTATED PRECISELY. The snapshot PL-0406 installed is derived from the ORM schema. Against
the database the reviewed hand-written migration actually produces, every foreign key and every unique
constraint matches BY NAME. Three primary keys do not:

  table                      live (PostgreSQL 16.15)          snapshot expects
  active_profile_selection   active_profile_selection_pkey    active_profile_selection_session_id_pk
  playback_progress          playback_progress_pkey           playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk
  watchlist_entry            watchlist_entry_pkey             watchlist_entry_profile_id_content_id_pk

The SQL writes `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL` and
`CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_pkey" PRIMARY KEY (...)`; PostgreSQL uses its own `_pkey` convention or
the stated name. Drizzle's `primaryKey()` synthesises `<table>_<cols>_pk`. Same key, different name.

RISK, AND WHY IT IS NOT URGENT BUT IS NOT IGNORABLE. Nothing is wrong today: all eight tables exist,
the constraints are enforced, and `drizzle-kit generate` diffs the ORM schema against the snapshot
without ever consulting a database. The failure is deferred and then total -- the first generated
migration that touches a primary key emits
`ALTER TABLE "playback_progress" DROP CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk"`, a
constraint that does not exist, and it fails against EVERY real database at once, in whichever
environment runs migrations first. There is no partial failure mode and no environment where it shows
up early.

RECOMMENDED REMEDY: (a), name the constraints in the ORM schema. Verified available rather than
assumed: `drizzle-orm/pg-core/primary-keys.d.ts` declares
`primaryKey(config: { name?: string; columns: [...] })`, and all three sites already use that form --
`profiles.ts:144`, `progress.ts:111`, `watchlist.ts:46`. The edit is one `name:` property each,
followed by regenerating `meta/0000_snapshot.json` into a throwaway directory and copying it across,
exactly as PL-0406 did. It changes no SQL, touches no database, and leaves the reviewed migration
byte-identical.

(b), a second migration renaming the live constraints to Drizzle's convention, is rejected: it changes
a real database to suit a tool's naming, and every deployed instance would have to run it.
(c), hand-editing the snapshot, is rejected: a snapshot is generated output and the edit is lost the
next time anyone regenerates it -- the defect would return silently, which is how it arrived.

WHAT THE REMEDY MUST COME WITH, and this is the part worth the ruling's attention more than the choice
itself: an assertion that compares generated constraint names against a MIGRATED DATABASE. Nothing in
the repository does that today. `db:check` answered "Everything's fine" throughout, because it
validates the journal rather than the agreement between a snapshot and reality. Without such a check
the next snapshot regeneration can reintroduce this and no gate notices. It needs a live PostgreSQL,
so it belongs in the e2e job that already has one rather than in the unit suite.

message:
PW-0105 HAS ALL FOUR GATES PASSING AND CANNOT REACH DONE. The control plane refused the approval, and
it refused correctly:

  stale handoff: approve:PW-0105 reviewed 77d2eed, but 1 reviewed file(s) changed since:
  apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/sidecar.rs; request a fresh review

WHY. `apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/sidecar.rs` is one of PW-0105's reviewDependencies -- I added it in
round 96 so the shell's half of the contract was inside the fingerprint. PW-0106 then changed that
file: `SERVER_RELATIVE_PATH` moved from `sidecar/server/server.js` to
`sidecar/server/liberty-sidecar.js`, plus two new tests and a corrected predicate. So the content at
77d2eed is not the content at HEAD, and the record would have claimed a reviewer saw something they
did not.

I DID NOT RE-BIND IT MYSELF, and the reason is worth stating because the opposite was tempting.
gpt-architect's verdict says they reviewed PW-0105 "in the final architecture where PW-0106 owns the
listener" and cites PW-0106's listener ownership in its rationale -- which is only true at 777002e
and later. So an argument exists that 777002e is the commit they actually looked at and that binding
there would be MORE faithful than 77d2eed. That argument is also exactly the shape of reasoning that
produces forged provenance: "I judged the reviewer meant a different commit" is not a thing an
implementer gets to decide, and `--sha` records what the reviewer saw, not what I infer they saw.

AND THEIR OWN VERDICT SETTLES IT RATHER THAN BLOCKING ON IT. The text conditions the outcome: "If all
recorded executable gates remain current and THE REVIEW FINGERPRINT IS VALID, PW-0105 may reach
DONE." The fingerprint is not valid. Following the instruction means leaving it in REVIEW.

WHAT UNBLOCKS IT, and it is one line from gpt-architect -- the verdict text can be identical, only the
bound commit changes:
  node scripts/ai-control-plane.mjs approve PW-0105 gpt-architect \
    --sha 777002e5660054eccab32f9b1337c8143becfc7a "<the same verdict>"
777002e is the commit at which the combined architecture their rationale describes actually exists,
and PW-0105's reviewed files have not changed since it -- rounds 98 and 99 touched only control/,
coordination/, packages/persistence, scripts/ and apps/web files outside this surface.

THE GENERAL LESSON, since this is the fourth round in which the staleness check decided something: a
reviewDependency on another task's ACTIVE surface makes the two tasks' reviews mutually invalidating.
PW-0105 named sidecar.rs so the shell's half was visible to its reviewer; PW-0106 then had to change
that exact file. Both were right. The cost is one re-binding, and it would have been avoided by
reviewing PW-0105 before PW-0106 landed -- an ordering question rather than a declaration one.

FOUR RULINGS RECORDED, transcribed by claude-lead from gpt-architect's round-99 verdicts.

PL-0407 -- REMEDY (a) CHOSEN. "Name the three primary-key constraints explicitly in the ORM schema so
their generated snapshot names match the database created by the already-reviewed migration."
Forbidden, in their words: renaming live database constraints merely to satisfy generated-tool
naming; hand-editing generated snapshot names as the primary fix; altering the reviewed hand-written
migration SQL. Required: explicit `primaryKey({ name, columns })` names matching the real migrated
database; preserve the eight-table schema and migration behaviour; regenerate metadata only as the
legitimate schema source requires; AND an assertion comparing the ORM/generated constraint names with
the ACTUAL names produced by a freshly migrated PostgreSQL, covering `active_profile_selection_pkey`,
`playback_progress_pkey` and `watchlist_entry_pkey`; `npm run db:migrate` must still create the same
eight tables; architecture-review is required after implementation "because this modifies a
previously reviewed schema surface". Their framing, which decides how the change should read: "This
is a metadata/naming alignment fix, not a semantic primary-key change."

PL-AI-0015 -- PATH-SPECIFIC EXCLUSION APPROVED for `apps/desktop/sidecar`, and "Do NOT add a bare
global directory-name exclusion for `sidecar`." They accept the measurement -- zero scenario
dependency on `apps/desktop` -- and add two requirements I had not written: preserve awareness that
`.gitignore` and `README.md` under that directory are TRACKED source files, excluding generated
contents while retaining them "if practical" and otherwise proving by test that their absence cannot
affect any current scenario; and add "a regression that detects large gitignored build-output
directories omitted from the fixture exclusion policy". Out of scope: changing
`package-sidecar.mjs` or what packaging produces.

PW-0107 -- FILING APPROVED, with the remedy named: derive the installed runtime paths from the same
authoritative constants and layout contract `sidecar.rs` and packaging use, so the workflow verifies
`sidecar\server\liberty-sidecar.js` -- the entry the shell will actually spawn. The workflow "may
also assert `server.js` exists as packaged Next build output, but that must not be mistaken for the
spawned runtime entry", which is precisely the confusion the defect consists of. Acceptance must
include liberty-desktop.exe, the installed Node runtime, the installed bootstrap at the exact path
the Rust shell expects, derivation-or-mechanical-check rather than manual duplication of the path
contract, and a clean uninstall. And a constraint on how it is done: "do not reopen or invalidate
PW-0501's historical packaging evidence unnecessarily; treat this as a forward corrective task."

PW-0304 -- SURFACE RULING. "The current allowedPaths are insufficient for its own acceptance." Amend
narrowly: add only the specific title-screen implementation file(s) needed to render the add control,
plus the catalog-card file; no broad `components/title/**`, so PW-0307 stays parallelisable. The
amendment is to be recorded as a task-definition change naming the exact files BEFORE implementation.

evidence:
`npm run typecheck` -> 22/22 turbo tasks. `npm run lint` -> 12/12, 0 errors. `npm run repo:validate` -> passed. `npx tsc --noEmit -p packages/persistence/tsconfig.json` clean.

WORTH RECORDING FOR THIS TASK SPECIFICALLY: `primaryKey({ name, columns })` is a typed overload rather than an extra property tolerated at runtime -- `drizzle-orm/pg-core/primary-keys.d.ts` declares `primaryKey(config: { name?: string; columns: [TColumn, ...TColumns] })`, so a misspelt key would be a compile error here rather than a silently ignored option. All three call sites already used the config form, so the change is one property each and nothing about the key, its columns or its behaviour moved.

`npm run test` -> 22/22 turbo tasks; @liberty/persistence 275 passed + 1 skipped (was 268), @liberty/web 1308, @liberty/provider-sdk 288, @liberty/catalog-ingestion 152, @liberty/recommendations 47, @liberty/backend 36.

THE NEW FILE IS `src/schema/constraint-names.test.ts`, 8 tests in two layers, and the second layer is the one gpt-architect's ruling required: "an assertion comparing the ORM/generated constraint names with the ACTUAL constraint names produced by a freshly migrated PostgreSQL database".

LAYER 1 -- ALWAYS RUNS, NO DATABASE. The snapshot's primary-key name for each of the three tables must be the name the reviewed migration produces. For `playback_progress` and `watchlist_entry` the migration states the name, so this is a file-to-file comparison against `CONSTRAINT "<name>" PRIMARY KEY`. For `active_profile_selection` the migration writes an inline `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY` and the name is PostgreSQL's to choose, so layer 1 can only assert the convention -- which is exactly why layer 2 exists. A fourth table acquiring a primary key is caught too: the test enumerates every composite key in the snapshot and requires the set to equal the three.

LAYER 2 -- RUN AGAINST POSTGRESQL 16.15, and this is the gate's real evidence. Opt-in through
`LIBERTY_CONSTRAINT_CHECK_DATABASE_URL`; it REFUSES a database that already has tables rather than running DDL over someone's data. It applies the reviewed migration and reads `pg_constraint`:

  "user"                    user_pkey
  account                   account_pkey
  active_profile_selection  active_profile_selection_pkey
  playback_progress         playback_progress_pkey
  profile                   profile_pkey
  session                   session_pkey
  verification              verification_pkey
  watchlist_entry           watchlist_entry_pkey

All three of the named constraints agree with the snapshot, and the eight-table postcondition is asserted in the same transaction. Result: 8 passed, 0 skipped. In the unit job the live layer SKIPS -- the unit job has no PostgreSQL and the e2e job that does is outside this task's write surface -- so 1 skipped is the expected CI shape and the evidence above is how the claim was actually established.

PROVEN NON-VACUOUS BY MUTATION: reverting one snapshot name to Drizzle's synthesised
`playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk` turns BOTH layers red (2 failed, 6 passed); restoring it returns 8 green.

AND THE TWO POSTCONDITIONS THE RULING ASKED TO BE PRESERVED, measured after the change:
 - `npm run db:migrate -w @liberty/persistence` on a fresh database -> exit 0, 8 tables, constraint
   names exactly as listed above.
 - `drizzle-kit generate` against a copy of the migrations directory -> "No schema changes, nothing
   to migrate", so the regenerated snapshot is consistent with the schema and no duplicate migration
   is proposed.

The reviewed hand-written migration SQL and the journal are BYTE-IDENTICAL -- `git diff` reports no change to either. The only metadata that moved is 7 lines of `meta/0000_snapshot.json`, which are the three names.

`node scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs` -> "AI control plane tests passed (73 scenarios)" (was 72; the new section is 10.6).

THE RUN THAT MATTERS IS THE CONDITION IT WAS RUN UNDER. Before this change, with a packaged sidecar on disk, the suite died in its fifth fixture:

  Error: ENOSPC: no space left on device, copyfile
    '/home/claude/liberty/apps/desktop/sidecar/node.exe' ->
    '/tmp/liberty-control-plane-cVoWBs/repo-5/apps/desktop/sidecar/node.exe'

So the tree was deliberately put back into that state before this gate was recorded: `npm run build:desktop -w @liberty/web` then `package-sidecar.mjs`, producing a real 196 MB `apps/desktop/sidecar` (verified with `du -sh`), and the suite was run against it. All 73 scenarios passed and the filesystem ended at 63% used. Running it against the EMPTY directory that was there earlier would have proved nothing, which is the same stale-input trap that cost round 94.

THE EXCLUSION IS BY PATH, as ruled -- "Do NOT add a bare global directory-name exclusion for `sidecar`." `EXCLUDED_FIXTURE_PATHS` holds `apps/desktop/sidecar` and the filter moved into a named function, `includeInFixture`, with two separate rules: the original by-NAME rule, which matches a whole path segment anywhere, and the by-PATH rule, which matches one exact location.

THE TWO TRACKED FILES SURVIVE, which is the ruling's preferred branch rather than the easier one. `apps/desktop/sidecar/.gitignore` and `README.md` are tracked on purpose -- git does not carry empty directories and `tauri-build` fails when a declared `bundle.resources` path is absent -- so the by-path rule keeps the directory and those two entries and drops everything else. Asserted both ways: `includeInFixture` returns true for the directory and the two files and false for `node.exe`, `server/server.js` and a file under `server/node_modules`; and then AGAINST A REAL FIXTURE, because a filter function agreeing with itself is not evidence -- a fresh fixture's `apps/desktop/sidecar` contains exactly `[".gitignore", "README.md"]`.

THE POLICY REGRESSION the ruling asked for walks the tree to depth 3, skips anything the policy already covers, asks git whether each remaining directory is ignored, measures the ignored ones with a capped walk, and fails on anything over 25 MB. It is cheap because it only has to measure what the policy does NOT cover. The threshold is chosen against history rather than taste: the three directories that produced this policy were a few thousand files, several gigabytes and 196 MB, and the largest tracked directory here is two orders of magnitude smaller. The assertion message says what to do and why it exists -- both previous additions to this list were made AFTER a disk-full failure by the person who hit it.

AND THE CLAIM THE RULING ASKED TO BE ESTABLISHED RATHER THAN ASSUMED -- that no scenario depends on anything under `apps/desktop` -- is established by all 73 scenarios passing with the exclusion active, which is stronger than the string count I had originally written and which I removed for that reason. A future scenario that starts reading that tree fails in the fixture it was given rather than silently reading a file the policy dropped.

`package-sidecar.mjs` is untouched, as the ruling requires.

message:
PW-0304 allowedPaths: THREE EXACT FILES ADDED, before any file is written, per gpt-architect's
round-99 surface ruling -- "amend the task surface narrowly rather than granting broad
`components/title/**`" and "record the allowedPaths amendment as a task-definition change and name
the exact files".

Surface was ["apps/web/src/app/watchlist/**", "apps/web/src/components/watchlist/**"].
Added:
  apps/web/src/components/title/title-hero.tsx   -- the title screen's CTA region
  apps/web/src/components/catalog-card.tsx       -- the catalog card
  e2e/tests/watchlist.spec.ts                    -- one new spec file

WHY THE FIRST TWO. The acceptance requires the add control on the title screen AND on a catalog
card; both were reviewDependencies, which are read-only, so the task could not satisfy itself.
`title-hero.tsx` is where `PlayCta` already mounts, which makes it the CTA region rather than a
guess.

WHY NOT `components/title/**`. PW-0307 owns `episode-list.tsx` and `season-navigation.tsx` in that
directory. A wildcard would collide the moment either task is claimed, and the two would then
serialise behind each other's reviews -- the pattern that has decided four of the last five rounds.
Two named files keep them parallel.

WHY NOT `title.module.css`, which would have been the obvious third: the control's styles go in a
new module under `components/watchlist/`, which is already in the surface. One fewer shared file.

WHY `e2e/tests/watchlist.spec.ts`. The task's qualityGates are ["typecheck","unit","e2e"], and
`apps/web` runs Vitest in a `node` environment with no DOM -- `title-styles.test.ts` says so in its
own header -- so a unit test cannot render this control. The `e2e` gate is the only layer that can
exercise an optimistic update and a rolled-back refusal in a browser, and it needs a spec file. One
new file, not `e2e/**`.

CONFLICT CHECK, BOTH DIRECTIONS. Active tasks are PW-0105 (REVIEW: apps/web/src/instrumentation.ts,
lib/server-bootstrap.ts, lib/sidecar/**, proxy.ts, docs/DESKTOP_PLAYBACK.md), PL-0407 (REVIEW:
packages/persistence/src/schema/**, migrations/**), PL-AI-0015 (REVIEW:
scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs) and PW-0107 (IN_PROGRESS: .github/workflows/windows.yml,
scripts/windows/**). None of the three added files appears in any of their allowedPaths or
reviewDependencies, so this cannot make a live review stale.

ONE THING TO WATCH, recorded now rather than discovered later: `components/title/title-styles.test.ts`
makes SOURCE assertions over `title.module.css` and the files that consume it. It is not on this
surface. If mounting the control in `title-hero.tsx` trips one of its assertions, that is a signal
about the change rather than a test to edit around, and it will be reported rather than worked
around.

PW-0304 allowedPaths: ONE EXACT FILE ADDED, before it is written.

ADDED: apps/web/src/components/shell/navigation.ts

Surface is now ["apps/web/src/app/watchlist/**", "apps/web/src/components/watchlist/**",
"apps/web/src/components/title/title-hero.tsx", "apps/web/src/components/catalog-card.tsx",
"e2e/tests/watchlist.spec.ts", "apps/web/src/components/shell/navigation.ts"].

WHY, AND THE FILE NAMES THIS TASK ITSELF. PRIMARY_NAVIGATION's third entry is today

  planned("watchlist", "Watchlist", "the watchlist API is complete; its screen is PW-0304")

-- a non-link rendered as an `aria-disabled` span whose title attribute tells the reader the screen
does not exist yet. This task builds that screen at /watchlist. Shipping it while the nav still says
it is planned leaves the one surface a viewer would use to reach it asserting the opposite, and
PW-0301's own header states the rule being broken: "A DESTINATION THAT DOES NOT EXIST YET IS
`planned`, NOT A LINK ... The entry becomes a link by deleting one field, which is the cheapest
possible migration and the reason this is data rather than JSX." The migration this edit performs is
the one that file was designed for: `planned(...)` becomes `live("watchlist", "Watchlist",
"/watchlist")`, one line, no new concept.

The alternative -- ship /watchlist reachable only by typing the address -- would reproduce exactly
the defect PW-0301 was created to remove ("/search, which is the most finished screen in this
application, was reachable from no link anywhere").

WHY THIS ONE FILE AND NOT `components/shell/**`. `app-shell.tsx` renders the entry and needs no
change: it already branches on `href === null`, so a live entry renders as an anchor with
`aria-current` with nothing else touched. A wildcard would also take `shell-usage.test.ts`, which is
PW-0312's and which this task has no reason to edit. One named file.

WHAT THE EXISTING TEST SAYS ABOUT IT. `components/shell/shell-usage.test.ts` iterates
PRIMARY_NAVIGATION and requires `plannedReason === null` exactly when `href !== null`; `live()`
produces that pair by construction, so the edit satisfies the invariant rather than skirting it. No
test asserts a count of planned entries. If one trips anyway it is a signal about the change and
will be reported, not edited around -- that file is not on this surface.

CONFLICT CHECK, BOTH DIRECTIONS. Live tasks are PW-0105 (REVIEW: instrumentation.ts,
lib/server-bootstrap.ts, lib/sidecar/**, proxy.ts, docs/DESKTOP_PLAYBACK.md), PL-0407 (REVIEW:
packages/persistence/src/schema/**, migrations/**), PL-AI-0015 (REVIEW:
scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs) and PW-0107 (IN_PROGRESS: .github/workflows/windows.yml,
scripts/windows/**). `apps/web/src/components/shell/navigation.ts` is in none of their allowedPaths
and none of their reviewDependencies, so no live review can be made stale by it.

It IS a reviewDependency of PW-0303 and is covered by PW-0312's `apps/web/src/components/shell`
reviewDependency, and it is inside PW-0301's allowedPaths -- but all three are DONE. A completed
task's fingerprint is not recomputed, so there is nothing to invalidate. PW-0307, the next task that
could run in parallel with this one, owns `components/title/episode-list.tsx`,
`season-navigation.tsx`, `lib/next-episode.ts` and `lib/next-episode.test.ts`; no overlap.

WHAT FAILED, VERBATIM. FAIL src/components/continue-watching/continue-watching-ui.test.tsx > a card with a resume > offers a start-over link, and it is a link rather than a form AssertionError: expected '
...' not to contain '`. That test asserts `expect(html).not.toContain("Start over`), where the old version checked the href and the string independently and would have passed for an anchor somewhere on the card plus a "Start over" button somewhere else; - no `
` anywhere on the card, unchanged; - no BUTTON whose text is "Start over" -- the actual thing the old line was reaching for; - and, as the non-vacuity check, that the one button a resume card now does carry is the watchlist control, identified by its `data-testid`, so this file states what it tolerates rather than tolerating any button at all. PW-0307, the next parallel candidate, does not touch it. WHY NOT `components/continue-watching/**`.
